title: The Covenant Sealed in Blood, and a Meal Before God
summary: Moses reports the LORD's words and the people agree with one voice. He writes the words down, builds an altar with twelve pillars, has young men offer sacrifices, and reads the Book of the Covenant; when the people vow obedience, he sprinkles the blood of the covenant on them. Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders then see the God of Israel and eat and drink in his presence, and Moses goes up into the cloud of glory for forty days and forty nights.
story: Chapter 19 offered the covenant, chapters 20-23 set out its terms, and chapter 24 seals it. This is the formal making of the Sinai covenant, the relationship on which the rest of the Old Testament's history depends; when the prophets later accuse Israel of breaking the covenant, this is the ceremony they have in mind. The chapter also turns the book. From verse 12 Moses goes up to receive the tablets, and during his forty days on the mountain God gives him the instructions for the tabernacle (chapters 25-31). Below, the people who twice promised to do all that the LORD had spoken will soon make a golden calf (chapter 32). Their promise is sincere and short-lived.
historical:
Agreements in the ancient Near East were confirmed with ritual: an oath, a written copy of the terms, a public reading, witnesses, sacrifice, and often a shared meal. The Sinai covenant has every one of these. The words are written down (verse 4), twelve standing stones serve as memorials or witnesses for the tribes, the scroll is read aloud (verse 7), the people swear, the blood is applied, and the leaders eat on the mountain. Hittite treaties directed that the text be deposited before the gods and read publicly at intervals, and Deuteronomy later commands that the law be read to all Israel every seventh year at the Feast of Tabernacles (Deuteronomy 31:10-11).

Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's eldest sons, appear here among the privileged few; Leviticus 10 records their death for offering unauthorized fire, a sober reminder that nearness to God does not guarantee faithfulness. The seventy elders anticipate the seventy on whom the Spirit rests in Numbers 11. Joshua appears again as Moses' attendant, and Hur, who held up Moses' hands against Amalek (17:12), is left with Aaron to settle disputes while Moses is away.
cultural:
Blood carried the meaning of life in Israel's world: “the life of the flesh is in the blood” (Leviticus 17:11). Dividing the blood between the altar, which stood for God, and the people bound both parties in a bond of life and death. Some interpreters compare the older covenant rite of Genesis 15, where animals were cut in two and the one who passed between them invoked death on himself if he broke faith. Others stress the cleansing sense of blood, which later consecrates the priests (29:20-21), so that the people are both bound to God and made fit to belong to him.

A shared meal was the ordinary way to seal an agreement, as when Isaac feasted with Abimelech after their oath (Genesis 26:30) and Jacob ate with Laban on the mountain (Genesis 31:54). Here the meal is eaten in the presence of the divine King, probably from the meat of the peace offerings. The vision in verse 10 describes only what lies under God's feet, a pavement like sapphire and clear as the sky. The stone is probably lapis lazuli, the deep blue stone prized in Egypt and Mesopotamia and linked with the heavens, rather than the gem now called sapphire.
literary: The chapter wraps the covenant ceremony (verses 3-8) inside the ascent of the mountain (verses 1-2 and 9-11), holding the people below and their leaders above in one frame. The people answer twice: after hearing the words spoken (verse 3), and again after hearing them read from the scroll (verse 7), where the vow grows to include “we will be obedient,” literally we will hear. The approach to God is graded: the people at the foot, the elders partway up, Joshua accompanying Moses, and Moses alone entering the cloud, a pattern later built into the tabernacle's courtyard, holy place, and inner room. Verses 15-18 echo the creation week, with six days of waiting and a call on the seventh, and they introduce the glory that will fill the finished tabernacle in the book's final scene (40:34).

outline.t: The summons to worship at a distance
The covenant confirmed with words, sacrifice, and blood
Israel's leaders see God and eat and drink
Moses goes up to receive the tablets
Forty days in the cloud of glory

doctrines.note: The covenant is made in words that are written, read, and accepted, and it is sealed in blood. God binds himself to Israel and Israel to him, and the terms are public, so the people know exactly what they have promised.

The blood on altar and people shows that a relationship between a holy God and a sinful people rests on a life given, not on the people's vow alone. Their promise will fail within weeks, and what holds them to God then is his mercy.

God makes himself known here in word and in presence: the Book of the Covenant read to all, and the glory seen by the elders and by all Israel as a consuming fire. Scripture and the living God are held together, neither replacing the other.

words.note: Dam, blood. In the Old Testament blood stands for life, and above all for life given up in death. Here it dominates the ceremony: half splashed on the altar, half kept in bowls and sprinkled on the people with the words “This is the blood of the covenant” (verse 8). Zechariah 9:11 recalls the same covenant blood as the ground of God's promise to free his people.

Kavod, glory. The root means heavy or weighty, and in ordinary speech it named a person's honor, wealth, or importance. Used of God, it names the visible splendor of his presence, here like a consuming fire within the cloud. The glory that rests on Sinai will fill the tabernacle in 40:34, so the mountain's presence travels with Israel.

Shakan, to settle or dwell. The glory of the LORD settles on the mountain (verse 16), and the same verb supplies the word mishkan, dwelling place, the Hebrew name for the tabernacle in the chapters that follow. Later Jewish writers used a related term, Shekinah, for God's dwelling presence among his people.

christ: At the Last Supper Jesus took the cup and said, “This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many” (Mark 14:24), deliberately echoing verse 8. Luke records the cup as “the new covenant in My blood” (Luke 22:20), recalling Jeremiah's promise that God would “make a new covenant with the house of Israel” (Jeremiah 31:31). Hebrews 9:18-20 quotes verse 8 and argues that even the first covenant “was not put into effect without blood,” pointing ahead to Christ's own. The meal on the mountain, where Israel's leaders see God and eat and drink, anticipates both the Lord's Supper and “the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9), where the people of God eat in his presence. Moses' forty days and nights on the mountain are echoed by Jesus' forty days of fasting in the wilderness (Matthew 4:2), a thematic link rather than a stated fulfillment.

hard.q: The elders saw the God of Israel. Doesn't Scripture say no one can see God and live?
hard.a: Verses 10-11 say the elders saw the God of Israel and survived, yet in 33:20 God tells Moses, “You cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live,” and John writes, “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18). The text signals the tension itself: it describes nothing of God's form, only the pavement under his feet, and it notes with evident surprise that God did not lay his hand on them. Interpreters handle this in several ways. Many distinguish seeing God in a mediated form, a vision or a manifestation of his glory, from seeing his essence or unveiled face, which no creature can survive. Christian readers have often added that such Old Testament appearances were revelations of God through the Son, who, in John's words, “has made Him known.” Ancient translators felt the difficulty as well: the Greek Septuagint renders verse 10 as saying they saw the place where the God of Israel stood. Every approach agrees that what the elders saw was real and also partial, a gift of grace that let them live.

questions: Israel promised twice to do everything the LORD had said and broke the promise within weeks. What does that suggest about the limits of good intentions in a relationship with God?
The covenant was sealed with blood and celebrated with a meal. How does this background change the way you hear Jesus' words over the cup?
Moses waited six days in the cloud before God spoke. What do you do with seasons when God seems to make you wait?
